clue.text: Oddly easier having first dealt with revolutionary Big Mac ingredient

indicators.note: the letters just picked out must have the next two pieces placed ahead of them

parts.note: a claim or an order that has been dealt with has been processed
Che Guevara, the Argentine-born revolutionary

indicators.note: oddly points to the letters in the first, third and fifth places of the word that follows

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of easier

explanation.surface: A fussy diner, having already eaten, tackles a revolutionary new burger more easily.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is read back to front: the odd letters of 'easier' come last, with PROCESSED and CHE placed first. A Big Mac is McDonald's best-known burger.
explanation.definitionFit: The Big Mac famously contains a slice of factory-made processed cheese among its fillings, so it is an example of an ingredient.

clue.text: Steep climbs with number on crew who can deliver

indicators.note: in a down clue something that climbs reads from bottom to top, so the word is turned round

parts.note: to sop is to soak or steep something in liquid
two is a number
to man a ship is to crew it

explanation.surface: Sheer ascents, done with a numbered team who can supply what is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steep' looks like an adjective for a slope; here it is the verb meaning soak, which gives SOP, read upwards as POS.
explanation.definitionFit: A postwoman's job is delivering the mail, so she is someone who can deliver letters and parcels.

clue.text: Taxing cash after banks rejected gold put up by America

indicators.note: in a down clue putting something up means writing it from the bottom upwards
the banks of a word are its two outer letters, and rejecting them leaves only the inside

parts.note: cash is money
or is the heraldic word for gold
the US, the United States of America

explanation.surface: Taxation of money once the banks have refused gold reserves offered by America.
explanation.walkthrough: MONEY with its outer letters gone leaves ONE; OR turned upwards gives RO; then US.
explanation.definitionFit: Taxing in the sense of demanding or burdensome is a close synonym of onerous, as in an onerous duty.

clue.text: Occasionally meant wound is recorded

indicators.note: occasionally means only now and then, so only every other letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of meant
wound in the sense of coiled or turned into a roll

explanation.surface: A wound inflicted by accident, now and again, has been officially noted down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' looks like an injury; it is the past tense of wind, as in wound up into a roll.
explanation.definitionFit: To be enrolled is to have one's name entered on a register or list, that is, recorded.

clue.text: Sierra regularly parking under branch

indicators.note: in a down clue being under something means sitting below it, so this part follows the first

parts.note: Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every second letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of parking

explanation.surface: A car parked beneath a tree branch in the Sierra mountains on a regular basis.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprig is a small shoot or twig, a little branch cut from a plant.

clue.text: Shock retrospective rescued gallery

indicators.note: a retrospective looks backwards, so the word that follows is read from its end

parts.note: rescued means saved
the Tate is the famous London art gallery

explanation.surface: Surprise as a gallery's retrospective exhibition rescues it from closure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like an art show, which fits the gallery; it is the instruction to read SAVED backwards as DEVAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To devastate someone is to shock and overwhelm them with grief, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Hard once a state captures a soldier

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: to capture something is to hold it inside, so the state wraps round the next letter

parts.note: the USSR, the Soviet state that no longer exists
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tough former nation takes a soldier prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once a state' means a former state, the Soviet Union, which wraps round A after H.
explanation.definitionFit: A hussar is a light cavalry soldier, originally from Hungary, so a kind of soldier.

clue.text: Involve ball going into middle of green when spun

indicators.note: spinning turns a thing round, so the whole result is read backwards
going into the middle of something means being placed inside it between its halves

parts.note: lime is a shade of green
an orb is a ball or sphere

explanation.surface: A golf or snooker shot: the ball reaching the middle of the green with spin on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like a golf green, which suits the ball, but it is a shade of the colour; and 'spun' turns the whole thing round, not just the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: To embroil someone is to involve them in a conflict or difficult situation.

clue.text: Pitchers meanwhile throw the quicker balls last of all

indicators.note: the last of all the words means the final letter of every word in the run

parts.note: the final letters of the five words

explanation.surface: Cricket: the bowlers meanwhile save their faster deliveries for the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitchers' and 'throw' push towards baseball or bowling, but the pitchers are jugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A ewer is a large jug with a wide spout, and a pitcher is another word for a jug.

clue.text: The woman making rare move to become Match of the Day pundit?

parts.note: she is the pronoun for the woman

indicators.note: making the letters move means shifting them into a new order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A woman makes the unusual career move into football punditry on the BBC.
explanation.walkthrough: Match of the Day is the BBC's long-running football highlights show; Alan Shearer, the former England striker, is one of its pundits. The question mark flags that this is one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Shearer is a regular expert analyst on the programme, so the surname names one of its pundits.

clue.text: Workable if making a design essentially obvious

indicators.note: making the letter into something else means swapping that letter out for the new pair

parts.note: a workable plan is viable

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so only its middle letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of design

explanation.surface: A design is workable if it makes its essential purpose clear.
explanation.walkthrough: The A of VIABLE is replaced by SI, the heart of 'design'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something visible can be seen, and something obvious is plain to see, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Try to get whiskey glasses

parts.note: Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet
two round letters that look like a pair of spectacles

explanation.surface: Attempting to obtain whiskey tumblers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glasses' looks like drinking glasses to go with the whiskey; it is spectacles, drawn as two rings.
explanation.definitionFit: To woo is to court someone or seek their support, trying to win them over.

clue.text: Biggest part of Last Leg is starting with introduction from Adam Hills nailing MPs?

indicators.note: starting with means the following words come at the front, ahead of the letter just found

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the biggest part of a word, read as its capital letter, is the upper-case initial

parts.note: the capital L, the largest letter of the word

indicators.note: an introduction is the opening, so only the first letter of the name is used

parts.note: the first letter of Adam
tors are rocky hills, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: Comedian Adam Hills, host of the TV satire The Last Leg, skewering politicians in his opening.
explanation.walkthrough: The Last Leg is a Channel 4 topical comedy show hosted by Adam Hills; 'Biggest part' playfully means the capital letter of 'Last'. LEG IS comes first, then L, A and TORS.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of Parliament make the country's laws, so they are examples of lawmakers; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Long-term strategy to control most of factory

indicators.note: most of a word means all of it except its final letter

parts.note: to master something is to control it
a plant is an industrial factory

explanation.surface: A business plan to take control of the larger part of a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: A masterplan is a comprehensive plan for the future, which is a long-term strategy.

clue.text: Scramble panda car using energy to cover every area with time to complete previous case

indicators.note: scrambling mixes things up, so the letters are jumbled into a new order
completing means coming at the end, so this piece is tacked on last
using one letter in place of another signals a swap of letters inside the phrase
covering a letter means laying another over it, so each such letter is swapped out

parts.note: taken as written
E is the symbol for energy in physics
T is the abbreviation for time
a is the abbreviation for area; every A in the phrase is replaced

explanation.surface: A police officer is told to rush the patrol car around every district in the nick of time.
explanation.walkthrough: A panda car is British slang for a small police patrol car. Each A in it becomes E, giving PENDECER, which is jumbled and finished with T.
explanation.definitionFit: In law a precedent is an earlier decided case that guides later rulings, so it is a previous case.

clue.text: Channel took off by the sound of it

indicators.note: judging by the sound tells us the spelling is chosen to match how the word is said

parts.note: a plane that took off flew

explanation.surface: A TV channel seemingly took off, judging by the sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' suggests a broadcaster or waterway; here it is a duct.
explanation.definitionFit: A flue is a duct or passage carrying smoke and gases from a fire, so a kind of channel.

clue.text: Appearance made by em-cee performing without right info

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so these letters go round the next pieces
performing is acting out, so the letters are worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A master of ceremonies makes a stage appearance without the right information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like lacking, but here it means outside. Gen is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: Emergence is the act of coming into view, which is an appearance.

clue.text: Rose in bloom was obvious

parts.note: to rise from a seat is to stand, so rose gives stood
flowers that are out are in bloom

explanation.surface: A rose in flower was conspicuous in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the flower, and 'in bloom' encourages that; it is the past tense of rise.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that stood out was conspicuous, which means it was obvious to everyone.

clue.text: Having removed embarrassing smell, scientist brought back stink

indicators.note: bringing something back sends it the other way, so the letters read from the end
having removed something means taking those letters away from the word

parts.note: a boffin is British slang for a scientist
BO, body odour, is the classic embarrassing smell

explanation.surface: A scientist got rid of a whiff of body odour, but brought back a stench.
explanation.walkthrough: BOFFIN loses BO to leave FFIN, which is reversed. Niff is British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A niff is an unpleasant smell in British slang, which is a stink.

clue.text: Bother to hide business leader's confrontation

indicators.note: hiding something means keeping it inside, so one word is wrapped round the other

parts.note: faff is British slang for time-wasting bother
a chief executive officer leads a business

explanation.surface: An awkward attempt to conceal the boss's argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bother' is a noun here: faff is British slang for fuss or hassle, as in 'what a faff'.
explanation.definitionFit: A face-off is a direct confrontation between rivals, as at the start of an ice hockey play.

clue.text: Stupidly repeat cycle ignoring tip from Noddy Holder

indicators.note: doing something stupidly suggests a muddled result, so the letters are jumbled
ignoring the tip of a word means leaving out its end letter from the letters used

parts.note: taken as written
the tip, or end letter, of Noddy

explanation.surface: A complaint about Slade's singer, playing the same song on a foolish loop.
explanation.walkthrough: Noddy Holder is the singer of the British glam-rock band Slade, so 'Holder' pretends to be his surname. Drop the Y from 'repeat cycle' and jumble the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A receptacle is a container, something that holds whatever is put in it, so a holder.

clue.text: Hundreds taking time on motorway in China

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it, so it comes first
taking something in means holding it inside, so the pair goes round the rest

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, and the plural asks for two of them
an era is a period of time
the M1 is England's main north-south motorway

explanation.surface: Hundreds spend time on the expressways of China.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1 of the M1 is read as the Roman numeral I. 'China' at the start hides its lower-case sense, the porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: China is fine porcelain, which is a type of ceramic ware made from fired clay.

clue.text: Primate is upset with bishop, say, touring Italy

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting a word turns it upside down, reading from the bottom

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: touring a place means going all around it, so one word encloses the other

parts.note: a bishop is an example of a man, a chess piece
I is the international vehicle code for Italy

explanation.surface: An archbishop is upset that a bishop is touring Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' looks like a senior churchman, matching the bishop; it is the ape sense. IS turned up gives SI, then MAN surrounds I.
explanation.definitionFit: Simian means relating to apes and monkeys, and as a noun names an ape or monkey, which is a primate.

clue.text: Perhaps Prince covers No. 1 from Peter Gabriel — ultimately having a try in various keys?

indicators.note: to cover something is to wrap round it, so the prince's name goes outside

parts.note: Prince Archie, son of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, is one example

indicators.note: the number one letter of a word is its very first

parts.note: the first letter of Peter

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the name is kept

parts.note: the final letter of Gabriel
a go is a try

explanation.surface: Prince performs a cover of a Peter Gabriel song, trying it out in various musical keys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince' and 'keys' suggest the singer and music; the prince is Archie, and the keys are low islands, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: An archipelago is a group of islands, and keys (cays) are small low islands, so a chain of them fits.

clue.text: Journalist supporting American politician is excited

indicators.note: in a down clue the supporting piece sits underneath, so it goes after the rest

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
an MP is a Member of Parliament
ED, the editor, is the crossword's usual journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter backing an American politician is thrilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Amped is informal for excited and full of energy, like an amplified signal.

clue.text: Reversing Skoda estate, somewhat lost

indicators.note: reversing goes backwards, so the run of letters is read from right to left
somewhat means a part of something, so the letters sit inside the run of words

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A driver backing a Skoda estate car is rather disoriented.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate is the British term for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: To be at sea is an idiom for being confused and bewildered, that is, lost.

clue.text: Kid's newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kid's' reads as a child's paper; the apostrophe-s is just 'is' joining two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: To rag someone is to tease them, as to kid is; a rag is also slang for a trashy newspaper.

clue.text: Sketch crocodile for opening

indicators.note: an opening is a start, so this piece goes at the front of the word

parts.note: pro means in favour of
a crocodile is a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs, which is a file

explanation.surface: Drawing a crocodile to begin an art lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crocodile' is not the reptile: in Britain it is a line of schoolchildren walking two by two.
explanation.definitionFit: A profile is a short descriptive article or an outline drawing of a face, both senses of a sketch.

clue.text: Mackintosh possibly breaks — how many bits are missing?

indicators.note: with bits missing at both ends, only a stretch from the middle of the run is left

parts.note: the letters run across the words

explanation.surface: A raincoat tears, and someone asks how many pieces have gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mackintosh' looks like a raincoat; it is Sir Cameron Mackintosh, the theatre producer behind Les Misérables and Cats.
explanation.definitionFit: A showman is a flamboyant producer of entertainment, and Cameron Mackintosh is a famous example.

clue.text: The idiotic teen clarified it

indicators.note: something idiotic is senseless, so the letters are muddled into a new order

parts.note: taken as written before rearranging

explanation.surface: A dim teenager explained the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' looks like the start of the sentence but is the definition on its own, the word 'the' itself.
explanation.definitionFit: In English grammar 'the' is the definite article, the determiner pointing to a specific thing.
